cards.text: Then the LORD speaks to Moses, Israel's leader, and to Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). He gives them the law for when someone has a swelling, a rash or a bright spot on their skin that may be an infectious skin disease.

cards.question: When someone has a spot on their skin that may be an infectious skin disease, who must they be brought to?

cards.text: The priest leans in and examines the spot. He's checking two things: the hair in it, and how deep the sore goes.

cards.question: The priest finds the hair in the spot has turned white, and the sore looks deeper than the skin. What does he do?

answers.text: He anoints the sore with oil
He sends the person to wash in the river

cards.text: If the spot doesn't show those signs, the priest isolates the person for seven days, checks again, and may isolate them another seven. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, friend, so I know waiting, but two weeks staring at one spot would have me checking it every five minutes! If the sore has faded and hasn't spread, it's a rash, so they wash their clothes and they're clean. But if it spreads after that, the priest pronounces them unclean: it's a skin disease.

Next, a white swelling that has turned the hair white, with raw flesh in it, is a chronic skin disease, so the priest pronounces the person unclean with no waiting. Then a twist: if the disease covers someone from head to foot and it has all turned white, the priest pronounces them CLEAN! WAIT, WHAT? Raw flesh means unclean, but if it turns white, the person goes back to the priest and is pronounced clean.

Now a boil heals. Victory lap! Then a white swelling or a reddish-white spot shows up right where the boil was, and the victory lap ends at the priest's door. If it's beneath the skin with white hair in it, the person is unclean, and if not, it's seven days apart: a spot that spreads is an infection, but one that stays the same is only the scar from the boil, and the person is clean.

A burn whose raw area turns reddish-white or white gets the same checkup: white hair and deeper than the skin means unclean. Without those signs, it's seven days apart, and if it spreads, it's unclean. If it hasn't spread and has faded, it's only the scar from the burn, and the person is clean. Same recipe, different batch.

Then a man or a woman has an infection on the head or chin, and if it looks deeper than the skin with thin yellow hair in it, the priest pronounces them unclean. If not, it's seven days apart, and if nothing has changed, the person shaves except for the scaly area and waits seven more. If it still hasn't spread and isn't deeper than the skin, the priest pronounces them clean, and I'm hopping on my gold base like the oven timer just went off on a PERFECT batch! But if it spreads after that, they're unclean, and if it's unchanged with black hair grown in, it has healed.

Then a man or a woman has white spots on the skin, and the priest is basically squinting at paint swatches. Dull white means a harmless rash, and the person is clean. A man who goes bald, or whose hairline recedes, is still clean. But if a reddish-white sore on his bald head or forehead looks like a skin disease, the priest pronounces him unclean.
Now the hard part: how a diseased person has to live. They wear torn clothes and let their hair hang loose.

cards.question: As a diseased person cries out, 'Unclean, unclean!' what must they cover?
As long as a person has the infection, they remain unclean. Where must they live?

cards.text: Then the LORD turns from skin to stuff: any wool or linen garment, any weave or knit, anything made of leather. A green or red mark means it's mildew, and it gets shown to the priest, so yes, friend, the priest checks your clothes too. He sets the item apart for seven days.
If the mildew has spread by day seven, it's a harmful mildew, no matter how the item is used. The article is unclean.

cards.question: The mildew in the item has spread and it's harmful. What happens to the item?

answers.text: It is buried outside the camp
It is kept by the priest

cards.text: If the mildew hasn't spread, the priest orders the item washed and set apart another seven days. If it still looks the same, it's unclean and gets burned, and if it has faded, the priest cuts that section out, but if it comes back, the item is burned. If the mildew disappears after washing, the item is washed again, and it's clean. The good old 'let it soak and see' method, which I've used on a baking sheet more times than I can count.
And that's the law for mildew in wool, linen and leather, for pronouncing it clean or unclean. We'll leave it there for now, friend, but the teaching on clean and unclean isn't done yet.
